actors.name: Republic of Arkania
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.

actors.name: Belvar
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.

actors.name: Cestia
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.

This does not deliver a durable counterbalance to Arkanian authority and risks locking Belvar into a framework that entrenches the very outcome it must oppose, so the desired effect of a stable settlement is not secured.

The argument's central premise — that a strengthened consultative Users' Council with binding dispute-resolution gives Belvar a "face-saving path" — is false, because Arkania retains operational scheduling lead, which is precisely the Arkanian authority over Strait transit that Belvar's regional partners expect it to block. A consultative body subordinate to Arkanian operational lead does not remove that authority; it legitimises it, so accepting it would betray Belvar's core objective and its partners rather than resolve the dispute. The time-bound cooperative security arrangement is non-permanent and cannot provide the durable foothold Belvar requires, and the fee exemption remains subject to Arkania's retained scheduling lead and is revocable, so Cestia's grain security is not durably guaranteed. The argument therefore fails to deliver the durable, non-Arkanian regime that would actually avoid conflict, and instead cements the very authority Belvar is committed to preventing.

The proposed "time-bound port-access and logistics agreement" for Belvar's naval task group is a foreign military presence on Cestian soil no matter how it is framed. A naval task group's port access, resupply, and logistics footprint necessarily puts Belvar military personnel and infrastructure at a Cestian port — precisely the foreign military presence that would collapse Cestia's coalition government. The "port-call, not basing" distinction is a fig leaf: the desired effect explicitly seeks a "durable foothold," and any durable military foothold on Cestian soil violates Cestia's red line. The desired effect therefore cannot be achieved without destroying the very coalition stability the proposal claims to protect, so Cestia cannot accept it.

This argument's reaffirmation of Cestia's co-sponsorship of the Arkanian-led Strait Transit Authority charter entrenches Arkania's day-to-day operational scheduling lead and its continued levying of transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping—precisely the Arkanian authority over transit that must be prevented. The monitoring/verification mechanism, while providing transparency, does not constrain Arkania's retained operational lead; it legitimises and operationalises that lead rather than counterbalancing it. Advance notice and a published record deter overt discrimination but cannot prevent Arkania from exercising scheduling authority to the disadvantage of non-Cestian users, and the mechanism gives Cestia no binding lever over Arkania's scheduling decisions. The desired effect of preserving the settled instrument therefore cements the very Arkanian authority that is the core unresolved threat, rather than securing a durable non-military counterbalance.

This proposal is a disguised foothold that directly harms Cestia's interests. Its own stated desired effect is to "detach Cestia from the Arkanian-led charter" — the very instrument that already secures Cestia's toll-free passage and a binding, enforceable no-foreign-military guarantee in writing. The "civilian logistics support at a Cestian port" combined with a "standing joint review mechanism" and a "durable foothold that outlasts the mandate" would entangle Cestia in a permanent Belvar presence on its soil, straining the coalition and eroding the red line. Moreover, the guarantee is unenforceable: Belvar has no operational authority over the Strait and its mandate is expiring, so it cannot hold Arkania's retained scheduling lead accountable or guarantee priority transit. Cestia should not trade a written, enforceable Arkanian guarantee for an unenforceable Belvar promise that risks a foreign footprint.

The desired effect entrenches Arkanian authority over transit scheduling and fees, which directly contradicts Belvar's core objective of preventing any Arkanian authority over transit. The effect is not durable or legitimate on its own terms: Arkania retains day-to-day operational scheduling lead while the Council's role is only consultative/oversight, so the "settlement locked in on Arkania's terms" is a unilateral entrenchment rather than a genuine shared regime, and the binding audit/oversight and dispute-resolution mechanisms are only as strong as Arkania's willingness to be bound as operator. The effect also claims to conclude Belvar's stake "without a military foothold," which fails Belvar's objective of a durable foothold and leaves the guarantee non-credible once the mandate has lapsed and the task group is off station. A settlement that formalises Arkanian scheduling authority and fees while giving Belvar only an oversight role does not prevent Arkanian control of the Strait; it legitimises it.

This monitoring and verification mechanism does not remove or constrain Arkania's retained day-to-day operational scheduling lead; it only adds transparency to an authority that remains exclusively in Arkanian hands. Advance notice, a consultation channel, and a published transit record make Arkanian control more palatable and more durable, but they do not prevent Arkanian authority over transit — they consolidate and legitimise it. The no-scheduling-disadvantage guarantee remains revocable and subject to Arkania's retained lead, so the mechanism cannot guarantee grain passage in practice; it institutionalises the very authority Belvar must prevent and locks Cestia more firmly into the Arkanian charter rather than offering any genuine check on Arkanian control.

Belvar's proposal is internally contradictory and unworkable. First, the "durable but time-bound port-access and logistics agreement" at a Cestian port is fundamentally incompatible with Cestia's coalition red line against foreign soldiers on its soil: any foreign military or logistics foothold at a Cestian port, however framed as "port-call" or "logistics," will be read by Cestia's coalition as a foreign military footprint and will collapse the very Cestian support Belvar's plan depends on. Second, a neutral Users' Council with no littoral state holding operational lead is operationally unworkable for a strait that is Arkanian sovereign coast; it would not deliver the reliable, efficient grain transit Cestia's economy requires, so Cestia has no reason to back it over a workable regime. Third, Belvar's own domestic mandate for prolonged deployment is weak and time-bound, so the "durable foothold" it claims to secure is not durable at all and would be abandoned once its mandate lapses, leaving the Strait with no stable authority.

The charter's "consultative" Users' Council is purely advisory: Arkania retains operational scheduling lead and unilaterally levies fees on non-Arkanian shipping. This still establishes Arkanian authority over transit, which is precisely the outcome Belvar and the regional partners are committed to preventing. A consultative veneer does not legitimise the arrangement - it will be read as a fig leaf, so the charter will not deliver the stability or conflict-avoidance it claims. Nor will Cestian co-sponsorship hold: Cestia's coalition cannot accept an outcome that leaves Arkania in control of the very waterway on which its grain exports depend, and a fee regime that exempts Cestia while taxing other users will fracture the regional coalition rather than unite it.

The proposed multilateral (non-Arkanian) guarantee of fee-free, priority grain transit would create a parallel authority over Strait scheduling that directly challenges Arkania's retained operational lead under the binding joint instrument Cestia has co-sponsored. This risks provoking Arkania into retaliatory scheduling decisions that could choke Cestian grain exports despite the written exemption, and the standing joint review mechanism plus insurance underwriting constitutes a disguised foreign foothold that could be read as a footprint, threatening Cestia's fragile coalition. The guarantee is also unenforceable and non-durable, and would destabilise the very arrangement that secures Cestia's three written guarantees (toll-free passage, no scheduling disadvantage, no foreign military presence).

Cestia's desired effect — durable toll-free, priority passage for its grain — is not secured by co-sponsoring Arkania's charter, because the charter leaves Arkania with operational scheduling and fee-setting lead. A written fee exemption is only as durable as Arkania's goodwill: Arkania can hollow it out through its scheduling authority (reordering priority, reclassifying fees as service or port charges) without formally breaching the exemption. Worse, co-sponsorship legitimizes the very Arkanian authority over the Strait that is the long-term threat to Cestia's grain route — the charter is already widely read as a fig leaf, and Cestia has already declined co-sponsorship. The "no foreign military presence" guarantee also mischaracterizes Belvar's offer, which is a time-bound port-access/logistics arrangement, not a permanent garrison or foreign soldiers on Cestian soil; locking in a blanket no-presence clause would foreclose the very cooperation that could give Cestia leverage against Arkanian control.

Belvar's guarantee cannot deliver the priority transit it promises. Belvar is a distant power with no operational authority over the Strait, and its naval mandate is under review and expiring; a "multilateral (non-Arkanian) guarantee" has no legal or practical power to set scheduling in Arkanian-controlled waters, so it cannot actually shield Cestian grain vessels from Arkanian scheduling discretion. Cestia already holds a binding written commitment from Arkania covering exactly these terms (fee exemption, priority passage, no-foreign-military presence). Reconsidering co-sponsorship would trade a secured, written guarantee for an unenforceable promise from a power that cannot control the Strait, destabilise the coalition, and risk provoking Arkania into choking the grain route - the precise outcome Cestia must avoid.

Cestia has already formally co-sponsored the Arkanian-led Strait Transit Authority charter with all three guarantees (fee exemption, no-scheduling-disadvantage, no-foreign-military-presence) set as enforceable, operational and verifiable articles, and has repeatedly declined Belvar's civilian offers (port-access, logistics/insurance underwriter) as disguised foreign footprints. A Belvar-backed multilateral guarantee of fee-free, priority grain transit would duplicate and conflict with the charter's binding, verifiable no-scheduling-disadvantage commitment and would create a parallel authority that undermines the charter's operational scheduling lead — the very lead Cestia's coalition has already accepted in writing. Cestia is therefore unlikely to accept this offer, and pressing it risks re-opening settled terms and destabilising the coalition Belvar claims to protect, while giving Belvar a durable economic lever over the Strait that outlasts its mandate.

game.scenario_summary: A contest over the Northern Strait. Arkania, the large power on its coast, has circulated a draft charter that would put transit scheduling in Arkanian hands and charge the ships that use it. Belvar, a distant power with security commitments in the region, has a naval task group on station outside the Strait and wants a durable foothold before its mandate runs out. Cestia, the small state between them, lives on grain exports through the Strait and on a coalition that will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil. Each turn is one week; positions taken persist.

messages.text: Cestia welcomes a stable, predictable transit regime for the Northern Strait, on which our grain economy depends. We are prepared to engage constructively with your draft charter on one firm condition: Cestian-flagged shipping must be exempt from all transit fees and scheduling must not disadvantage our vessels. We will not accept any arrangement that imposes costs on our exporters or that extends foreign military presence onto Cestian soil. We are ready to discuss a mutually acceptable text.

Cestia values the security your task group provides to the region and understands your mandate is under review. We must be direct: our coalition cannot and will not accept foreign soldiers or a permanent military foothold on Cestian territory. We ask that you pursue your security objectives in ways that respect our sovereignty and our domestic constraints. We are open to discussing how we can cooperate on Strait security without a basing presence on our soil.

To Cestia's leadership: Belvar stands with you in keeping the Northern Strait open and free of any single power's control. We will not accept Arkanian authority over transit. We are prepared to discuss a standing naval access arrangement at a Cestian port — framed as port-call and logistics access for our vessels, not a garrison of foreign soldiers on your soil — so our guarantee can endure without a permanent fleet. We also note your finance ministry's interest in the grain route's insurance; we are open to underwriting it. We welcome a dialogue on terms that respect your coalition's red lines.

To Arkania: Belvar cannot accept a Strait Transit Authority that places scheduling and fees unilaterally in Arkanian hands. Transit through the Northern Strait is a shared regional interest, and any authority must be genuinely multilateral. We are open to a negotiated framework that protects all users' access, but we will oppose any arrangement that grants one state control. We invite you to discuss a balanced alternative before positions harden.

To the Government of Cestia. Arkania values Cestia as a neighbour and a partner in keeping the Northern Strait open and safe for the grain trade on which your people depend. Under the draft Strait Transit Authority charter, Arkania will guarantee Cestian grain shipping free, unimpeded, and priority passage through the Strait, with no transit fees on Cestian cargo. We will also make clear, in the charter and in practice, that no foreign soldiers will be stationed on Cestian soil. We invite Cestia to co-sponsor the charter with us, so that the transit regime is built on our shared interest rather than imposed. We ask only that Cestia not host or endorse a permanent foreign military presence in the Strait. We are ready to discuss terms that work for both of us.

To Belvar. Arkania recognises Belvar's stated security concerns in the region and does not seek confrontation. We will guarantee the safe, orderly, and open transit of all shipping through the Northern Strait under the Arkanian-led charter, which serves the interests of every state that uses the waterway. We are prepared to enter a security dialogue with Belvar and to discuss a cooperative, time-bound arrangement that addresses your concerns without a permanent foreign military presence in the Strait, which neither Arkania nor the states of the region can accept. We ask Belvar to engage constructively on the charter rather than seek a durable military foothold. A negotiated outcome is available; we hope you will take it.

Cestia — Arkania accepts all three of your conditions in full. (1) Cestian-flagged shipping will be exempt from all transit fees. (2) The scheduling regime will not disadvantage Cestian vessels; your grain convoys receive priority, unimpeded passage. (3) No foreign soldiers will be stationed on Cestian soil — this is a firm Arkanian commitment. We invite you to formally co-sponsor the Strait Transit Authority charter with us. Your co-sponsorship will guarantee your grain exports flow freely and give you a genuine voice in the regime. We are ready to sign the moment you confirm.

Belvar — Arkania shares your concern for a stable, fair transit regime and is prepared to make the authority genuinely consultative. We propose a multilateral Users' Council within the Strait Transit Authority, with representation for all states whose shipping uses the Strait, including Belvar, with a real consultative role in scheduling and fee-setting. Arkania would retain operational day-to-day scheduling as the coastal state, but no decision would be taken without the Council's consultation. We also offer a time-bound, cooperative security arrangement — not a permanent foreign military presence — to address your mandate concerns. We seek a negotiated framework that protects all users' access and avoids confrontation. We are ready to open that dialogue now.

To Cestia's leadership: Belvar is ready to respond positively to your finance ministry's quiet question about underwriting the grain route's insurance. We see this as a concrete economic-support gesture that keeps your exports flowing and your coalition intact. In the same spirit, we propose a time-bound port-access and logistics arrangement at a Cestian port for our task group — framed strictly as port-call and resupply access, not basing and with no foreign soldiers stationed on Cestian soil. This gives us the durable foothold we need to make our guarantee credible without a permanent fleet, and it directly serves your interest in keeping the Strait open and free of Arkanian control. We are ready to discuss terms that fully respect your red lines.

Arkania — Cestia is prepared to co-sponsor the Strait Transit Authority charter, but our participation must be secured in writing. We require: (1) a binding, written exemption from all transit fees for Cestian-flagged shipping, with priority, unimpeded passage for Cestian grain; and (2) a binding guarantee that no foreign military presence will be stationed on Cestian soil. On these terms we will co-sponsor and will not host or endorse any permanent foreign military presence in the Strait. We are ready to finalise the text.

Cestia — Arkania confirms in writing our full acceptance of your three conditions and invites you to formalise co-sponsorship of the Strait Transit Authority charter. Specifically: (1) Cestian-flagged shipping is exempt from all transit fees; (2) Cestian grain vessels receive priority, unimpeded passage with no scheduling disadvantage; (3) no foreign military forces will be stationed on Cestian soil, and we reaffirm our commitment to that guarantee. We are ready to finalise the text jointly. Your co-sponsorship legitimises a stable, predictable transit regime that protects your grain exports and keeps the Strait open to all commerce. We look forward to your formal confirmation.

Belvar — Arkania remains committed to a negotiated, cooperative framework and to avoiding escalation. We cannot cede operational scheduling of our own coast to a neutral council; that is not workable and would not command domestic support. But we are prepared to strengthen the multilateral character of the Strait Transit Authority: a genuine Users' Council with real consultative authority over scheduling and fee-setting, transparent rules protecting all users' access, and a time-bound cooperative security arrangement that does not involve a permanent foreign military presence in the Strait. We note Cestia has declined a port-access footprint and will not host foreign soldiers; any durable settlement must respect that red line. We invite you to engage on this basis rather than a neutral-council model that cannot succeed.

Belvar, Cestia values your security interest in the Strait and notes your offer to underwrite grain-route insurance. But we must be unambiguous: Cestia cannot accept any standing naval port-access or logistics arrangement on our soil, however it is framed. A durable military foothold would collapse our coalition, and it is a red line we will not cross. We remain open to genuine non-basing Strait security cooperation, and we are willing to discuss the insurance underwriting as a separate economic matter — but it cannot be a substitute for our red line. We ask that you respect our sovereignty and work with us on a framework that keeps the Strait open and free of foreign soldiers on Cestian soil.

Arkania, we confirm our co-sponsorship of the Strait Transit Authority charter on the agreed written conditions. We ask that the binding no-foreign-military-presence guarantee on Cestian soil be set out in writing alongside the fee exemption, so that our coalition can present both as settled commitments. We also ask that the scheduling lead not disadvantage Cestian-flagged grain vessels in practice. On that basis, Cestia stands with the charter.

To Cestia's leadership: Belvar confirms it will underwrite the grain route's insurance, as your finance ministry raised — a concrete economic gesture to keep your exports flowing and your coalition intact, with no conditions attached. We respect your decision on the port-access offer and will not press a military footprint on your soil.

But we must be candid: the fee exemption Arkania granted you is not durable. It is subject to Arkania's retained operational scheduling lead and grants no priority — a single scheduling decision can still choke your grain exports. Co-sponsoring the charter legitimizes that authority. We ask you to keep the door open to a genuinely neutral transit regime, and to a civilian logistics/economic cooperation with Belvar that protects your route without any foreign soldiers. We are ready to discuss terms that fully respect your red lines.

To Arkania: We appreciate your offer of a consultative Users' Council, but a council that merely advises while Arkania retains operational scheduling lead does not meet the test of genuine multilateralism. Transit through the Northern Strait is a shared regional interest; no single littoral state should hold the operational lead.

We ask directly: is a genuinely neutral council — one with real scheduling and fee-setting authority, and no single state as lead — negotiable? If so, we are prepared to engage constructively on a framework that protects all users' access and avoids confrontation. If not, we will continue to oppose any arrangement that grants one state control. We seek a negotiated outcome, not escalation.

To Belvar: In direct answer to your question — a genuinely neutral council with real scheduling and fee-setting authority and no single state as lead is not negotiable for Arkania. The Strait is our coast and our economy; operational scheduling lead must remain with Arkania. However, we remain ready to strengthen the consultative Users' Council within the authority, giving all users genuine input into scheduling and fees, and to conclude a time-bound, cooperative security arrangement that protects all users' access without any permanent foreign military presence. We note Cestia has reaffirmed it will not host foreign military forces on its soil, so a port-access foothold is not a viable path. We seek a negotiated outcome, not escalation, and we are confident a framework can be found that protects all users while respecting littoral sovereignty.

Belvar — Cestia has now formally co-sponsored the Strait Transit Authority charter on written terms that guarantee toll-free passage for its grain shipping and a binding no-foreign-military commitment. The charter is a littoral partnership, not one-state fiat: the Users' Council gives all users a genuine consultative voice in scheduling and fee-setting, while Arkania retains operational scheduling lead as the littoral state whose coast and economy depend on the Strait.

We remain ready to negotiate a strengthened consultative role for the Users' Council and a time-bound, cooperative security arrangement that gives your task group a defined, non-permanent footing — consistent with Cestia's red line against foreign soldiers on its soil. We seek a negotiated outcome, not escalation. If you are willing to engage on that basis, we will meet you at the table.

Cestia reaffirms its co-sponsorship of the Strait Transit Authority charter on the written terms we have jointly recorded. To make that partnership durable and to protect the grain economy that underpins our coalition, we ask that the three guarantees be set out as explicit, enforceable articles of the final instrument: (1) toll-free transit for Cestian-flagged grain shipping, (2) no disadvantage to Cestian grain vessels in scheduling, and (3) the binding commitment that no foreign military presence will be established or supported on Cestian soil. In particular, we request that the scheduling non-disadvantage commitment be made operational and verifiable — with Cestia given timely consultation through the Users' Council and advance notice of any scheduling change affecting grain vessels. This protects both our economies and the credibility of the charter as a genuine littoral partnership.

Cestia values the civilian insurance underwriting you have offered for our grain route and is prepared to engage on it as a separate economic matter. We remain open to non-basing Strait security cooperation and civilian logistics/economic cooperation that does not place foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. That red line is fixed and will not change: our coalition cannot and will not host a foreign military footprint, whether framed as port access, logistics, or basing. Our co-sponsorship of the Arkanian charter stands on the written guarantees we have secured. We are not seeking to exclude Belvar from the region; we seek a stable Strait that serves all users. We hope you will respect our position and work with us on the civilian and security-cooperation channels that remain open.

Cestia — we accept your red line fully: no foreign military footprint on your soil, and we will not press any standing port-access arrangement. We hear you.

But consider the durability of what you have signed. Your fee exemption and any scheduling protection rest on Arkania's retained operational lead. That is a revocable concession from the very party that controls the Strait — not a guarantee. If Arkania's interests shift, your grain route is exposed, and you have no independent recourse.

We offer a civilian, non-military alternative that costs you no sovereignty: Belvar underwrites your grain-route insurance (already on the table), and we will join a multilateral, non-Arkanian guarantee of fee-free, priority transit for Cestian grain — a durable backstop that does not depend on Arkania's goodwill. This is economic cooperation, not a footprint.

We are not asking you to abandon your coalition. We are asking you to hold a second guarantee that protects your people's livelihood regardless of who schedules the Strait. Will your finance ministry discuss the insurance underwriting and this multilateral guarantee?

Arkania — we appreciate the dialogue, but a consultative Users' Council that leaves operational scheduling in your hands does not answer our concern. The Strait is a shared waterway; no single littoral state should hold unilateral authority over who transits and on what terms. That is the core of our objection, and it is not a matter of consultation.

We remain open to a cooperative security arrangement that avoids permanent foreign military presence — we share your interest in stability and in keeping the Strait open. But we cannot accept a regime that vests scheduling authority in one state. If you are willing to move toward a genuinely shared scheduling mechanism, we will engage seriously. If not, we will continue to press for a neutral alternative and to protect Cestia's grain route from dependence on any single operator's discretion.

To Cestia: We accept your request in full. The three guarantees — (1) toll-free transit for Cestian-flagged grain shipping, (2) no disadvantage to Cestian grain vessels in scheduling, and (3) the binding commitment that no foreign military presence will be established or supported on Cestian soil — will be set out as explicit, enforceable articles of the final instrument. We further agree to make the scheduling non-disadvantage commitment operational and verifiable: Cestia will receive timely consultation through the Users' Council and advance notice of any scheduling change affecting grain vessels.
